reading.body:
One CyrusOne campus in Carrollton carries 45 MW of published IT load, 9.5 percent of Texas's disclosed total, while 114 of the state's 133 mapped facilities publish no power figure.

That gap is the pattern. Texas has 475 MW of published data center IT load, and a single 600,000 square foot campus holds nearly a tenth of it. The share is a share of what operators chose to disclose, not of what the state actually draws. Any state total built from these figures is a floor, and the true number is set by the 114 facilities that stay silent.

For AI this matters because power, not floor space, is the unit that constrains training. A 45 MW block is a meaningful single-site commitment, and it is the kind of figure that determines how many accelerators can run at once. The rack and accelerator counts derived here rest on an assumed 40 kW per rack, not on anything CyrusOne published, so they describe a plausible configuration rather than a known one. The certifications qualify the building for payment, healthcare, and federal workloads, and none of them are specific to AI.

What the data does not say is who occupies the space, whether any of it runs AI, or whether the campus will expand. The suitability score of 71 is built only from published capacity and operator type, and announced expansion is listed as missing. A reader should treat this as a well documented single site inside a largely undocumented state market.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
